transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, what brings me in is... my sleep has just become completely unmoored lately. It's strange how things shift. At first, I was waking up after maybe two or three hours, just full of energy, drafting all these elaborate plans for the house. I was ready to go, you know? It reminds me of back when I was finishing my master's thesis in the late seventies—I used to pull all-nighters and feel invincible the next day. The campus was so quiet then, just me and the raccoons by the library. But now... now it's different. I just lie awake before dawn, staring at the ceiling, and my stomach is all tight. There's just no sense of rest anymore. It’s like that feeling you get when you’re waiting for a train that’s delayed, just this awful, hollow waiting. I used to take the train into the city all the time when I was working, before I retired. The 6:05 express. But yes, the sleep, it's just gone.
Have you ever experienced periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or felt unusually confident or creative, even if it was just for a few days?

Oh, yes. Yes, I have. In fact, just a little while ago, for weeks I felt almost... brilliantly optimistic. It was incredible, really, as if every obstacle in front of me was just completely trivial. I was drawing up those house plans I mentioned, and I just knew exactly how to fix the entire layout of the first floor to get more morning light. 

But the funny thing is, if anyone questioned my ideas—like my brother-in-law, who doesn't know the first thing about load-bearing walls—I just snapped at them. I got so furious, like they were actively trying to sabotage the only sensible man in the room! Which is ridiculous because he's an accountant. He's always been an accountant. He worked for a firm downtown... oh, what was the name... Arthur Andersen, maybe? No, no, they went under with that whole Enron mess back in the early two-thousands. I remember watching that on the news. It’s amazing how these massive corporations just crumble like a house of cards, isn't it? Just poof, gone overnight. All those pensions, just wiped out. I was very lucky my retirement was tied up in a state fund, frankly. 

But, ah, what were we saying? Yes, I felt very, very confident for a few weeks there.
How long did you feel that way—very confident, energetic, and optimistic—during that time you described?

Well, let me think... it went on for about five months. Yes, five whole months right after that terrible investment loss I took. For that entire time, I was no longer living like my usual retired self, not at all. Everything I did, every ounce of that energy, just revolved around trying to undo the financial damage. I was absolutely certain I could outsmart the market to get it all back. 

The stock market is a funny thing, isn't it? It’s all just numbers on a screen now. Back in the day, you actually had paper certificates. I remember when my father bought shares in General Motors, he had this beautiful, ornate piece of paper locked in his safety deposit box at the Chase Manhattan branch on 4th Street. That bank building is a coffee shop now. Can you believe it? They kept the old steel vault door and put little tables inside it. I went in there for an espresso a few weeks ago and they charged me seven dollars! Seven dollars for a thimble of coffee! And the barista had a ring right through his nose. I just don't understand the economy these days, people paying that kind of money for bean water when they can barely afford their mortgages. It makes you wonder where it's all heading, really.
After that five-month period of feeling very confident and energetic, did you experience a time when you felt down most of the day, lost interest in things, or had other symptoms of depression?

Yes, yes I did. It hit me like a ton of bricks right after that. Just... everything went gray. I used to spend whole afternoons at the art museum downtown, or I'd lose myself in my photography. I had a whole darkroom set up in the basement at my old house. And cooking! I used to love trying new recipes. But lately... I just look at my camera sitting on the shelf, or think about joining the bridge table at the community center, and I feel absolutely nothing. Nothing at all, except just how utterly exhausting it would be to even pretend I cared. 

It's a shame about the museum, really. They have a fantastic collection of impressionist works. Monet, Renoir, all of them. I remember taking my late wife there on our third date. We stood in front of this massive water lilies canvas for what felt like an hour. She wore this beautiful yellow dress with little white buttons down the front. You don't see dresses like that anymore. Everything now is just... sweatpants and those awful rubber clogs with the holes in them. Crocs, I think they're called? I saw a man wearing them at the grocery store the other day, right in the produce section, squeezing the avocados. How do you even know if an avocado is ripe? They're always hard as rocks and then suddenly they're mush. It's a very unforgiving fruit, the avocado. But yes, the photography and the museum... I just can't bring myself to care about any of it right now.
